smartLayerNotes.quality: Thinner layers (0.12 to 0.16 mm) smooth curved walls and take sanding or acetone smoothing well. Keep the floor near 0.1 mm, because thin layers cool fast and ABS needs each layer hot to bond.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Bias toward 0.2 to 0.28 mm on load bearing parts. A thicker bead holds its heat longer and needs less fan, which helps bonding in a warm chamber. Tests show under 8 percent tensile loss from 0.1 to 0.2 mm, so this is a reliability choice more than a strength gain.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Minimum layer time (12 s in Bambu profiles) stretches small thin layers. Keep the fan low and add a second part instead of shortening the layer time.

smartLayer.note: ABS prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu holds 100 C from the first layer. Prusa runs 100 C (80 to 110 by part size). If corners lift, raise the first layer bed 5 to 10 C before adding more squish. Let the bed and chamber soak 10 to 15 minutes first.
firstLayer.squishNote: Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa). A first layer of 0.25 mm or more at 120 percent line width holds better than a thin one (Ellis).

structure.wallsNote: Bambu Standard uses 2 walls and its Strength preset 6. Extra walls add stiffness, but thick solid sections build shrink stress in ABS, so stop at 4 for large flat parts.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 20 percent for housings and jigs. Bambu Standard is 15 percent grid and Strength is 25 percent.

supports.note: Same material ABS supports weld to the part and leave scars. Bambu Support for ABS is a release interface (support only, enclosed printer, drying optional, limonene dissolvable). HIPS gives a soluble interface on dual nozzle or multi material printers, but Prusa warns ABS and ASA partly dissolve in limonene, so keep the dip short and test a scrap. Prusa soluble presets use a top Z distance of 0 with 3 interface layers.

coolingGuard.note: Ellis uses at least 15 s for ABS. Orca generic uses 3 s, which is too short for small parts.

smartLayerNotes.quality: ASA keeps its matte finish and UV stability at 0.12 to 0.16 mm, and thin layers show off curved outdoor parts. Keep the floor near 0.1 mm, because ASA splits between thin layers as easily as ABS.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Bias toward 0.2 to 0.28 mm for outdoor brackets and housings. A thicker bead stays hot longer and needs less fan, which helps layer bonding in a warm chamber.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Minimum layer time is 10 to 12 s in Bambu and Prusa profiles. Keep the fan at 35 percent or less and add a second part when small layers slow down.

smartLayer.note: ASA prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa runs the first layer at 105 C and then 110 C. Bambu holds 90 to 100 C. Raise the first layer bed 5 to 10 C if corners lift.
firstLayer.squishNote: Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa). A first layer of 0.25 mm or more at 120 percent line width holds better than a thin one (Ellis).

structure.wallsNote: Outdoor parts gain more from 3 to 4 walls than from dense infill, and walls also shield the core from weather.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 20 percent for brackets and housings, 25 percent for the Bambu Strength preset.

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for ABS as compatible with ABS only, so test it on a scrap before ASA. Same material ASA supports weld and leave scars. Prusa warns HIPS is not suited to ASA supports because ASA partly dissolves in limonene, and a long dip hurts Prusament ASA layer adhesion.

coolingGuard.note: Ellis uses at least 15 s for ABS. Orca generic uses 3 s, which is too short for small parts.

smartLayerNotes.quality: BVOH only forms the support interface, so its layer height follows the model. Thin layers under PLA or PETG give a smoother underside, but BVOH under extrudes if forced thin.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Strength does not apply. BVOH is dissolved away, so use the layer height the model needs.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: BCN3D runs the fan at 50 to 100 percent and Orca generic at 100 percent with an 8 s minimum layer time. BVOH softens below 60 C, so keep the chamber cool and the fan on.

smartLayer.note: BVOH (water soluble support) prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa runs the bed at 60 C and BCN3D at 45 to 90 C. Follow the model filament's bed temperature. BVOH sticks much better to a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft than to bare PEI.
firstLayer.squishNote: No BVOH specific squish guidance. BCN3D says to use Magigoo adhesive for reliable bed adhesion when BVOH touches the bed.

supports.note: BVOH dissolves in water about twice as fast as PVA and leaves less residue. Prusa pairs it with PLA and calls it the only practical soluble support for PETG, and BCN3D also lists ABS, PA and PAHT CF15. Warm water speeds dissolving. Keep the spool sealed with desiccant, expect a larger purge on tool changes, and clean the hotend after long BVOH prints. Prusa's soluble interface preset uses a top Z distance of 0, 3 interface layers and 0.1 mm interface spacing.

coolingGuard.note: Generic PVA uses 4 s, BVOH 8 s, HIPS 6 s.

smartLayerNotes.quality: As a model, HIPS sands well and smooths in acetone, so 0.12 to 0.2 mm is plenty. As a soluble support it follows the layer height of the part it holds.
smartLayerNotes.strength: HIPS is a soft, low heat plastic and rarely the structural choice. When it is a model, 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle bonds well and prints faster than thin layers.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Orca generic runs a 6 s minimum layer time with the fan at 0 to 60 percent. When HIPS supports ABS, follow the ABS fan settings since both share the fan.

smartLayer.note: HIPS prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa recommends 100 to 110 C. All standard Prusa sheets give the best adhesion, and a brim helps on small contact areas.
firstLayer.squishNote: No HIPS specific squish guidance. Treat it like ABS.

structure.wallsNote: As a model, 3 walls keep the soft plastic from denting. As a support, walls follow the ABS part.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 20 percent as a model. Support structures use their own pattern.

supports.note: HIPS dissolves in limonene with no residue (10 to 20 s dip, then dry the part 24 h) and prints at ABS temperatures, which is why it is the classic ABS support on dual nozzle or multi material printers. Prusa warns ABS and ASA partly dissolve in limonene and rates printing HIPS supports as challenging. Prusa's soluble interface preset uses a top Z distance of 0 and 3 interface layers, Bambu's default is 0.2 mm. HIPS is not water soluble. Bambu Support for ABS is a non-soluble alternative.

coolingGuard.note: Generic PVA uses 4 s, BVOH 8 s, HIPS 6 s.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Unfilled PA12 can print at 0.1 to 0.16 mm for detail and holds thin features better than PA6 because it shrinks less. Dry it first.
smartLayerNotes.strength: PA12 bonds well between layers. Use 0.2 to 0.28 mm for functional parts, and keep the chamber warm rather than adding air.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Polymaker runs PA12-CF with the fan off. Profiles use a 2 s minimum layer time, so small layers slow down rather than needing fan.

smartLayer.note: Nylon 12 (PA12) prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.35 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Polymaker runs PA12-CF with the bed at 25 to 50 C on a garolite sheet or PVP glue. Bambu's general nylon guidance is 100 to 120 C on glued plates. Use the surface's own range.
firstLayer.squishNote: No PA12 specific squish guidance was found. Glue stick or garolite matters more than nozzle height.

structure.wallsNote: PA12 is tough and flexible, so 3 walls suit most functional parts. Extra walls help under bending load.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 30 percent. PA12 warps less than PA6, so denser infill is less risky.

supports.note: Nylon welds to nylon supports. Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (now discontinued) for CF and GF nylons and PET-CF and names Bambu ABS and ASA as alternatives. Bambu does not list PA12, so treat this as a proxy. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PA, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Unfilled nylon has no fiber to limit detail, so 0.1 to 0.16 mm works, but nylon looks matte at any height and wet spools ruin thin layers. Dry first.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Nylon fuses well between layers when it is hot and dry. Use 0.2 to 0.28 mm for load bearing parts, which also cuts the warping that comes from many thin layers.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Profiles run the fan at 0 to 30 percent with a 2 s minimum layer time. Nylon warps when cooled, so keep the fan low even on small layers.

smartLayer.note: Nylon 6 (PA6) and PA6/66 copolymers prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.35 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa recommends 110 C. Bambu says 100 to 120 C with glue stick on PEI or the Engineering plate. Garolite works at low or no bed heat with PVA glue (Polymaker).
firstLayer.squishNote: Nylon bonds chemically to a matched surface, so use glue stick on PEI and keep the nozzle at normal height. Wet nylon gives a foamy first layer that no squish setting fixes.

structure.wallsNote: Nylon is tough and flexible, so 3 walls give a good balance. Add walls for parts under bending load.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 30 percent. Nylon absorbs impact well, and dense solid infill mostly adds warping.

supports.note: Nylon welds to nylon supports. Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (now discontinued) for PA6-CF, PAHT-CF, PA6-GF and PET-CF, and names Bambu ABS and ASA as the alternatives. Bambu does not list unfilled PA6, so treat this as a proxy. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PA, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Chopped fiber limits fine detail and raises clog risk below about 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle. Keep the floor at 0.15 mm. A 0.6 mm hardened nozzle at 0.2 to 0.3 mm is Bambu's first choice.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Push toward 0.2 to 0.3 mm. Fibers align along each bead, so layer bonds are the weak plane. Fewer, thicker layers mean fewer bond planes, and hot dry filament matters more than layer height.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Bambu PA-CF profiles use a 2 s minimum layer time and Prusa PA-CF 20 s. Keep the fan at 30 percent or less, since cooling weakens nylon layer bonds.

smartLayer.note: Fiber filled nylon clogs at thin layers; keep at least 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa runs PA-CF at 115 C on smooth PEI and 100 C on textured sheets. Bambu holds 100 C on glued plates. Use glue stick on all PEI.
firstLayer.squishNote: Fiber filled nylon bonds hard to glued PEI, so normal nozzle height is enough. Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa).

structure.wallsNote: Fibers align along each bead, so walls carry the load and infill adds stiffness cheaply but little strength. CF parts gain little from denser infill.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 25 percent. Spend material on walls and top and bottom shells first. Lightweight parts do fine at 10 to 15 percent.

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (280 to 300 C, hardened nozzle, dry required, now discontinued) for PAHT-CF and PA6-CF, and names Bambu ABS and ASA as the alternatives. It is a support interface only. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PAHT CF15, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Glass fiber roughens the surface, so thin layers gain little. Keep the floor at 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle. Bambu recommends a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle for PA6-GF.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Push toward 0.2 to 0.3 mm. Glass fibers align along each bead and layer bonds are the weak plane, so fewer thicker layers and a hot, dry spool matter most.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Bambu PA6-GF uses a 2 s minimum layer time and a fan of 10 to 30 percent. Keep the fan low, since cooling weakens nylon layer bonds.

smartLayer.note: Glass filled nylon clogs at thin layers; keep at least 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu holds 100 C on glued plates and lists glue stick as required. Use the same bed temperature for every layer.
firstLayer.squishNote: Glass fiber nylon bonds hard to glued PEI, so normal nozzle height is enough. Do not squish harder to cure lifting corners (Prusa).

structure.wallsNote: Glass fibers align along each bead, so walls carry the load and infill adds stiffness cheaply but little strength. GF parts gain little from denser infill.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 25 percent. Spend material on walls and shells first.

supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PA/PET (280 to 300 C, hardened nozzle, dry required, now discontinued) for PA6-GF and names Bambu ABS and ASA as the alternatives. It is a support interface only. BCN3D lists BVOH as compatible with PA, but BVOH must be kept dry and needs a multi material printer.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Thin layers (0.12 to 0.16 mm) suit clear or glossy PC and small detail. They cool quickly at 270 to 280 C, so they need a warm chamber to avoid cracking between layers.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Bias toward 0.2 to 0.28 mm. A thicker bead keeps more heat and fuses better, and PC splits between layers when it cools fast or the chamber is cold.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Bambu PC uses a 2 s minimum layer time and Prusa PC Blend 20 s. Keep the fan at 10 to 25 percent and let small layers slow down instead of adding air.

smartLayer.note: Polycarbonate (PC) prints well from 0.3 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.35 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa runs 110 C first layer and 115 C after. Bambu says 100 to 120 C with glue stick on its plates. Use 110 C, and go to 115 to 120 C if corners lift.
firstLayer.squishNote: PC shrinks hard, so a clean, level bed and steady first layer matter more than extra squish (Prusa). Use glue stick as a release layer on PEI.

structure.wallsNote: PC is tough enough that walls carry most of the load. Add walls before adding infill, and avoid large solid blocks that build shrink stress.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 25 percent for functional parts. Solid or very dense infill raises warping in PC.

supports.note: No maker lists a release or soluble support for PC. Same material PC supports bond hard, so widen the top Z gap to 0.25 to 0.3 mm or use tree supports to limit contact. Bambu names ABS and ASA as its support filaments for nylon and PET based materials, but does not list PC.

smartLayerNotes.quality: PETG rounds off fine detail and strings on small features, so very thin layers buy less than in PLA. Use 0.12 to 0.16 mm on curved tops and keep 0.2 mm elsewhere. Bambu uses 0.1 mm with a wider 0.5 mm line for translucent PETG.
smartLayerNotes.strength: PETG layer bonding depends on heat, not layer thinness. Thicker layers (0.2 to 0.28 mm) keep more heat in the stack and tolerate the low fan PETG wants. Stay at or under 0.7 of the nozzle diameter.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Bambu sets a 12 s minimum layer time for PETG and a low fan, so thin layers on small parts slow down a lot. Printing several parts at once keeps the nozzle moving and reduces blobs.

smartLayer.note: PETG prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.2 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa runs the bed at 85 C for the first layer and 90 C after, with a 230 C nozzle first layer and 240 C after. Bambu runs 60 to 80 C, profile 70 C, for every layer.
firstLayer.squishNote: Do not squish PETG. Prusa says PETG bonds strongly to smooth PEI and needs glue stick as a separator, and a nozzle that is too low causes blobs and burnt specks. Raise Z offset a little if the first layer looks glassy and rough.

structure.wallsNote: Bambu says raise strength with walls up to 6 and infill up to 50 percent, and warns that more of both raises warping risk. Prusa says use more perimeters instead of more infill for solid parts.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 30 percent is enough for most parts. Above 50 percent adds warping without adding much strength (Bambu).

interfaceMaterials: Bambu PETG Basic or PETG HF (own support)
supports.solubleDissolve: water, several hours; PVA is not compatible with PETG
supports.note: PETG welds to its own supports, and Bambu says PETG supports on a PETG model are harder to remove and can mark the surface. Raise the top Z gap from the 0.2 mm default to about 0.25 mm (expert value) or use an interface filament with a zero gap: Support for PLA/PETG, or PLA Basic as interface only. Bambu says PVA is not compatible as support for PETG.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Carbon fiber hides layer lines, so thin layers add little. Keep the floor at 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm hardened nozzle: Prusa says composites clog more with thinner layers and smaller nozzles. On a 0.6 mm nozzle the same band is about 0.3 to 0.42 mm.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Fibers weaken the bond between layers, and PETG bonding depends on heat. Prefer 0.2 mm or thicker with a hot nozzle and low fan, and orient loads along the layers.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Bambu sets a 6 s minimum layer time and a fan of 5 to 40 percent (V3 sheet 0 to 60). Thin layers on small parts lose less to cooling than in PLA-CF but will still string if the nozzle waits.

smartLayer.note: Prusa gives 0.2 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle as the lowest optimal layer for carbon fiber PETG, so sleipnir has little room to go thinner.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu: 65 to 75 C, profile 70 C, with glue. Prusa lists 70 to 110 C for composites depending on the base plastic.
firstLayer.squishNote: Prusa: the first layer must be perfect or the nozzle clogs. PETG-CF still bonds to smooth PEI, so use glue stick on smooth sheets. Cold pull before printing and use a hardened nozzle of 0.4 mm or larger.

structure.wallsNote: Fibers align along the walls, so walls add stiffness. Extra infill gives little, and layers bond worse than plain PETG, so orient the load along the layers. Fibers cut warping, so more walls are safe.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 25 percent. Walls and orientation decide stiffness; Bambu's PETG guide advises walls of 6 or fewer and infill of 50 percent or less.

supports.note: Bambu's PETG guide names Support for PLA/PETG for PETG-CF and says PVA is not compatible with PETG. The mutual PLA and PETG interface guide excludes PETG-CF. Use a wider Z gap than for PLA if you support with PETG-CF itself, because it welds to its own supports.

smartLayerNotes.quality: PLA holds fine detail well, so thin layers (0.08 to 0.12 mm) pay off on domes, slopes and curved tops. Below 0.08 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle Bambu does not test quality and gains nothing.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Layer adhesion in PLA is weaker than in-layer strength. Keep layers at or under half the nozzle diameter (0.2 mm on a 0.4 nozzle). Going thinner does not bond better, going thicker than 0.3 mm loses about half the layer strength.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Thin layers on small parts hit the minimum layer time, so the printer slows down. Add a second part or raise the minimum layer time only if overhangs curl.

smartLayer.note: PLA prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.2 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu profile: 35 C on Cool Plate, 55 C on PEI. Prusa holds 60 C on PEI for every layer.
firstLayer.squishNote: Default first layer height is 0.2 mm on Bambu and Prusa. Ellis suggests 0.25 mm or more with a wider first line for a forgiving first layer. Fix adhesion by cleaning the plate before adding squish.

structure.wallsNote: Bambu and Prusa default to 2 walls. PLA is stiff and brittle, so load bearing parts want 4 or more walls before more infill.
structure.densityNote: Bambu default is grid at 15 percent and Prusa uses crosshatch at 15. The Bambu Strength preset goes to 6 walls and 25 percent. Gyroid works for even strength in all directions.

supports.solubleDissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C for PLA), several hours
supports.note: PLA on PLA supports need a Z gap of about one layer, and they peel off with tools. Bambu Support for PLA and PVA allow a zero gap for a cleaner underside. PLA and PETG do not bond well to each other, so either can serve as the other's interface.

coolingGuard.note: Use 8 s for silk and on printers whose profiles use it (Prusa Core One).

smartLayerNotes.quality: Carbon fiber gives a matte finish with almost invisible layer lines, so thin layers gain little. Do not go below 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle: Prusa says composites clog more with thin layers and small nozzles.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Fibers weaken the bond between layers, so keep layers near 0.2 mm and print hot. Thicker layers on a 0.6 mm hardened nozzle (0.3 to 0.4 mm) help feed and clog less.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: PLA-CF needs full fan except where Bambu turns the auxiliary fan off. Thin fast layers on small parts hit the minimum layer time, so allow 8 s or more.

smartLayer.note: Carbon fiber PLA clogs and gains little below about 0.15 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu lists 35 to 45 C with glue on Cool Plate, and profiles use 45 on Cool Plate and 55 on PEI.
firstLayer.squishNote: Prusa: the first layer should be perfectly fine, otherwise the nozzle clogs. Do a cold pull before printing and use a hardened steel nozzle of 0.4 mm or larger.

structure.wallsNote: Fibers align along the walls, so walls carry the stiffness. Extra infill adds little to a CF part. Layers bond worse than plain PLA, so orient the load along the layers.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 20 percent is enough. Walls and orientation decide stiffness, not infill density.

supports.solubleDissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours
supports.note: Bambu TDS lists Support for PLA. A CF surface hides support marks well. The mutual PLA and PETG support guide does not cover PLA-CF.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Matte finish hides layer lines, so a plain 0.2 mm layer looks finished. sleipnir pays off only on shallow slopes where the stair step still shows. Going to 0.08 mm rarely improves what the eye sees.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Same as PLA: keep layers at or under half the nozzle diameter. Matte fillers can lower layer bonding slightly, so favor 0.2 mm over 0.28 mm for parts that carry load.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Matte PLA prints fast (Bambu rates it under 300 mm/s). Thin fast layers on small parts hit the minimum layer time first, so add parts or accept the slowdown.

smartLayer.note: Matte PLA hides layer lines, so thin layers pay off mostly on shallow slopes and domes.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu TDS: 35 to 45 C with PVP glue. PEI plates take 45 to 65 C.
firstLayer.squishNote: Matte hides first layer blemishes on the visible bottom face less than on side walls. Use the PLA first layer and a clean plate.

structure.wallsNote: Matte parts are stiff and brittle like PLA. Use 3 or 4 walls for parts that carry load.
structure.densityNote: 15 percent covers display parts. Matte hides infill show through better than glossy PLA.

supports.solubleDissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours
supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PLA for matte. The Support for PLA/PETG mutual pairing guide does not cover PLA Matte. Contact scars are less visible on a matte surface than on gloss.

coolingGuard.note: Use 8 s for silk and on printers whose profiles use it (Prusa Core One).

smartLayerNotes.quality: Behaves like PLA for detail. Thin layers on curved tops help, and the toughening additives do not change the safe floor of 0.08 mm.
smartLayerNotes.strength: The point of PLA+ is better layer bonding and impact resistance. Keep layers at or under half the nozzle diameter and print hotter than plain PLA; thin layers alone do not add strength.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: PLA+ blends often run 5 to 10 C hotter than PLA, so thin fast layers keep more heat. Watch overhangs on small parts and allow a slightly longer minimum layer time.

smartLayer.note: PLA+ (tough PLA) prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.2 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu Tough+ and eSUN PLA+ use the PLA bed range: 35 to 45 C on Cool Plate, 45 to 65 C on PEI.
firstLayer.squishNote: Same as PLA: 0.2 mm first layer, clean the plate first, then add squish only if lines look round.

structure.wallsNote: Impact and layer bonding come from walls. Use 3 or 4 for clips and brackets before adding infill.
structure.densityNote: 15 to 25 percent is enough for most parts. Extra infill adds weight and warping risk more than strength.

supports.solubleDissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours
supports.note: Tougher PLA+ can bond harder to its own supports. Use a support interface filament, or raise the Z gap to 0.25 mm if supports leave scars.

coolingGuard.note: Use 8 s for silk and on printers whose profiles use it (Prusa Core One).

smartLayerNotes.quality: Silk shine hides layer lines, so the stair step shows up as dull bands on curved and sloped surfaces. Use 0.16 mm and let sleipnir go down to 0.12 mm there. Stay above 0.08 mm: at that height and high speed silk shows a fish scale pattern.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Silk layers are weak already (Z tensile about 18 MPa against 27 MPa in plane). Thinner layers do not fix that. Hotter nozzle and slower flow help the bond more than layer height.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: A thin layer that hits the minimum layer time makes the printer slow down and the surface changes from glossy to matte. Enable Don't slow down outer walls or print several parts at once to keep gloss even.

smartLayer.note: Silk shine hides lines, and Bambu keeps silk between 0.12 and 0.20 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu TDS: 35 to 45 C on Cool Plate, High Temp Plate or Textured PEI, with glue. Cool Plate SuperTack is not recommended.
firstLayer.squishNote: No silk specific rule. Use the PLA first layer and keep the first layer temperature equal to the print temperature (Bambu sets both to 235 in its silk guide).

structure.wallsNote: Walls do not add strength to silk that is weak between layers. Use 2 to 3 and print structural parts in PLA, PLA+ or PETG. Print the outer wall first if surface quality matters more than overhang accuracy.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 15 percent for display parts. Infill shows through thin walls only on translucent or light colors.

supports.solubleDissolve: room temperature or warm water (under 50 C), several hours
supports.note: Bambu lists Support for PLA for silk (55 degree max overhang). Supports leave dull patches on a glossy surface, so orient the display face away from supports and use an interface filament.

coolingGuard.note: Use 8 s for silk and on printers whose profiles use it (Prusa Core One).

smartLayerNotes.quality: PP has a waxy, low gloss finish, so thin layers gain little. 0.16 to 0.2 mm is a good detail setting and keeps warping in check.
smartLayerNotes.strength: 0.2 to 0.24 mm bonds well and keeps the part flexible. PP fuses to itself well when hot, but very thin layers cool and shrink fast.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Orca generic runs the fan at 100 percent with a 4 s minimum layer time, and Simplify3D says a fan is required. PP warps when cooled hard, so cut the fan to 30 percent or less if corners lift.

smartLayer.note: Polypropylene (PP) prints well from 0.25 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.25 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa recommends 85 to 100 C on its PP sheet. PP sticks well only to PP, so use the PP sheet or PP tape on smooth PEI. Simplify3D says PP tape can fuse to a part at high bed temperature, so drop the first layer temperature slightly or add a raft.
firstLayer.squishNote: Recreus suggests a 0.15 mm first layer at 10 C above normal and 10 percent wider lines for its PP, with a brim. Prusa asks for a 5 to 10 mm brim.

structure.wallsNote: Walls set the stiffness of a flexible PP part. Large flat solid areas shrink most, so keep them small.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 20 percent. Sparse infill lowers shrink stress and reduces warping on large parts.

supports.note: No maker lists a release or soluble support for PP in the sources found. PP sticks well only to itself, so supports fuse to the part where they touch, and PP bridges and overhangs sag because of its shrinkage. Design out overhangs above 45 degrees, keep bridges short, and widen the top Z gap to 0.25 to 0.3 mm for same material supports.

smartLayerNotes.quality: PVA is support only, so sleipnir should follow the model filament. Thin layers on the model do not need thin PVA layers away from the interface.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Strength is not a goal for PVA. Keep it at the model layer height so the interface lines up with the model surface.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: PVA runs slow (4 to 6 mm3/s) and keeps a 7 s minimum layer time, so it is rarely the layer time limit on the part. Keep the nozzle from sitting idle, because PVA degrades and clogs if left hot.

smartLayer.note: PVA (water soluble support) prints well from 0.2 to 0.7 of the nozzle diameter; Quality mode uses 0.3 to 0.5 and Strength mode 0.3 to 0.5, since parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.

firstLayer.bedNote: Prusa uses 60 C on smooth PEI or satin sheets. Bambu profiles use 45 C on Cool Plate and 55 C on PEI.
firstLayer.squishNote: Prusa says PVA and BVOH stick much better to PLA than to PEI. Start the support on a 1 to 2 layer PLA raft, or design so PVA never touches the bed.

structure.wallsNote: Not applicable. PVA prints only as support base or interface, never as a wall.
structure.densityNote: Prusa's soluble profiles use a rectilinear support base at 2 mm spacing with a 0.1 mm interface spacing. Bambu says avoid tree supports with PVA because they are tall, thin and collapse, and use normal grid supports.

supports.solubleDissolve: water; several hours to a dozen hours, warm water and agitation help, PLA models under 50 C, about 20 ml per gram
supports.note: Use PVA for the interface only when possible. Prusa's interface profile uses a top Z gap of 0, 3 interface layers and PVA on the interface; the full profile uses 5 layers and PVA for the whole support. Pairs with PLA (similar temperatures). Bambu says PVA is not compatible as support for PETG, so use BVOH there. Bambu lets you set PVA as both base and interface but advises grid, not tree, supports.

coolingGuard.note: Generic PVA uses 4 s, BVOH 8 s, HIPS 6 s.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Do not go thin with 85A. Thin layers and poor bridging leave holes (Prusa), and flow is very low. Bambu allows 85A only on 0.6 and 0.8 mm nozzles, so use 0.3 mm on a 0.6 mm nozzle and stay above about 0.2 mm.
smartLayerNotes.strength: Layer bonding in TPU is good. Layer height changes softness only through the wall and infill count. Thicker layers reduce how far the soft filament has to be pushed per mm of travel.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Flow, not cooling, sets the speed. At 2.2 mm3/s a 0.3 mm layer on a 0.62 mm line prints about 12 mm/s. Bambu's profile uses a 20 s minimum layer time.

smartLayer.note: Soft TPU feeds poorly at thin layers, so sleipnir stays at a third of the nozzle or more.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu profiles use 30 to 35 C. Prusa lists 60 to 75 C for flexibles, higher for large parts.
firstLayer.squishNote: Print the first layer very slowly with a light squish. Soft TPU deforms under the nozzle if too close, so tune Z on a first layer test. Use glue stick on smooth PEI.

structure.wallsNote: Softness depends on walls and infill. Keep walls and top and bottom layers low to preserve the give, and raise them only where the part must resist wear.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 20 percent keeps the part soft. Use rounder patterns that let the walls flex.

supports.note: Prusa asks for a Z gap of 0.3 mm and XY separation of at least 100 percent for flexibles, and lists support removal as difficult. Avoid supports on 85A and design overhangs away. If needed, use PLA and a little alcohol at the joint.

smartLayerNotes.quality: Do not go thin with TPU. Thin layers and poor bridging together leave holes and protrusions (Prusa), and flow is so slow that fine layers take very long. Use 0.2 mm and let sleipnir go no lower than about 0.16 mm.
smartLayerNotes.strength: TPU bonds well between layers already, so layer height is a comfort setting. Slightly thicker layers (0.2 to 0.28 mm) let the extruder push less speed for the same output and reduce jams.
smartLayerNotes.thinLayerCooling: Cooling is rarely the limit. Volumetric flow is: at 3.2 mm3/s a 0.2 mm layer prints about 38 mm/s and a 0.28 mm layer about 27 mm/s on a 0.42 mm line. Keep cooling low or use Bambu's 100 percent only where the profile says so.

smartLayer.note: Thin layers make TPU harder to feed and bond, so sleipnir stays at 40 percent of the nozzle or more.

firstLayer.bedNote: Bambu TDS: 30 to 35 C on Cool or High Temp plates with glue. Prusa lists 60 to 75 C for flexibles and says larger models may need a brim and a slightly higher bed.
firstLayer.squishNote: Print the first layer slowly and do not over squish, since TPU squeezes sideways and can feed badly. Use glue stick as a separator on smooth and satin PEI. Textured PEI needs no separator.

structure.wallsNote: Softness depends on walls and infill together. Prusa says raise walls and infill for strength and lower the wall and top and bottom layer count to keep the part flexible.
structure.densityNote: 10 to 20 percent for a soft part, 30 percent or more for a firmer one. Gyroid gives even give in all directions (expert).

supports.note: Prusa lists support removal as difficult and asks for a Z gap of 0.3 mm and XY separation of at least 100 percent, because close supports stick too hard to TPU. Avoid supports where possible. Bambu warns against many objects with supports on one plate because travel causes stringing. Whether Bambu Support for PLA/PETG works on TPU is not stated by a maker, so test it.

changes.why: sleipnir keeps the thinnest layers on domes, slopes and faces and prints straight walls thicker, which saves time without losing detail.
0.08 mm layers make layer lines almost invisible on small models. Bambu's 0.08 mm High Quality preset.
Slow outer walls keep sharp edges on tiny features.
Lower acceleration avoids ringing on small, fast direction changes.
Gentler motion on the visible wall.
Arachne varies line width to fill thin features like swords, fingers and horns that fixed width walls skip.
Keeps walls thinner than two lines instead of dropping them.
Supports only under the steepest overhangs. Fine layers bridge small overhangs on their own. Bambu's 0.08 mm preset uses 15 degrees.
Tree supports touch the model at small points and come off organic shapes more cleanly.
Organic trees grow around the model and are easier to remove from figures.
Tiny layers finish in seconds. Slowing down gives each layer time to cool so heads and spikes do not melt into blobs.
Bambu's finest 0.2 mm nozzle preset. Minimal layer lines.
Matches the 0.2 mm nozzle.
Thin lines need more walls for the same shell thickness. Bambu's 0.2 mm presets use four.

materialHints.note: PLA holds fine detail best. Matte PLA hides layer lines. PETG strings on small travel moves. Filled materials cannot go through a 0.2 mm nozzle.

advice.text: Tilt miniatures back 30 to 45 degrees so faces and details are not on the support side.
Print several minis per plate. More travel time per layer lets each one cool, the same effect as a minimum layer time.
Swap to a 0.2 mm nozzle for 28 to 32 mm miniatures when one is available. Do not use it with CF, GF or glow filament: the clog risk is very high.

changes.why: Adjusts outer wall spacing so the shell lands where the model says, and keeps layers more consistent.
Needed for inner, outer, inner wall order.
Orca recommends this order for the best dimensional accuracy: the outer wall is not pushed outward by an inner wall printed after it.
Slower outer walls track corners and small holes more closely.
Turns round holes into polygons sized for the nozzle, so bolts fit without drilling.
Pulls in the first layer so the base is not wider than the part. Bambu's X1 profiles use 0.15 mm.
Fine tunes the last layers so the part's total height matches the model.
Uses the measured hole error from this printer's tolerance test. Positive values make holes bigger.
Uses the measured outside error from the same test.
Scales the part in XY to cancel the shrink this material shows after cooling. Matters most for ABS, ASA, PC and nylon.

materialHints.note: Filled materials (CF, GF) shrink and warp less. ABS, ASA and unfilled nylon shrink the most; plan on shrink compensation.

advice.text: Print round holes with their axis vertical. Horizontal holes print as teardrops and come out undersized at the top.

economy.label: Save filament

changes.why: Adaptive cubic gets sparse deep inside the part and uses about a quarter less plastic than rectilinear.
Low infill is enough when the part carries no load.
Two walls keep the part stiff. Walls are the best strength per gram.
Lightning only supports the top surfaces and uses the least plastic of any pattern.
Four top layers still close the surface.
Slim trees use less support plastic than grid supports.

checks: Compare grams before and after in the slice summary and report the saving.
If the loaded spool has less filament than the job needs, say so before slicing further (Spoolman or AMS remaining weight).

changes.why: Each extra wall makes TPU stiffer. Two walls keep a phone case soft enough to fit over the edges.
Gyroid flexes about the same in every direction, so the part does not have a hard axis.
Low infill lets the part compress. Raise it for firmer parts.
TPU buckles if pushed fast. Orca's generic TPU is capped at 3.2 mm3/s and Bambu TPU 85A at 2.2.
Long retractions stretch and jam soft filament. Orca's TPU profiles use 0.4 mm.
With little retraction, fast travel is what keeps strings short.
A third wall firms up bumpers and feet that need to hold shape.
More infill for parts that carry weight, like printer feet.

advice.text: Print phone cases standing on the back face so the lip prints as clean walls.
Use a direct drive extruder. Bowden printers struggle with TPU 95A and rarely handle 85A.
Feed TPU from an external spool holder, not the Bambu AMS or AMS lite. Only products sold as TPU for AMS go through the AMS.
Dry TPU before printing; it is marked drying required.

changes.why: Dense walls leave fewer gaps for food to get into.
Slightly more plastic closes gaps between lines.
Concentric top lines follow the outline of a cutter or rim, leaving fewer crossing grooves.

materialHints.note: Prefer natural (uncolored) PETG or PLA from a maker that publishes food contact documents. Avoid styrenics and fiber filled materials.

caveats.text: Layer lines and gaps trap food and bacteria that washing cannot remove. Prusa does not recommend printed parts as food containers.
Brass nozzles can contain about 2 percent lead. Use a stainless steel nozzle for anything that touches food.
Most filament colorants are not certified for food contact, even when the base resin is.
A food safe epoxy coating seals the surface. Otherwise treat the part as single use, such as a cookie cutter used once.
Hot drinks and dishwashers soften PLA (about 55 C) and can deform PETG near 70 C.

advice.text: Require a stainless steel or hardened nozzle that is certified lead free. Ask if the printer still has a brass nozzle.

changes.why: Thicker walls resist sagging and creep when the part is warm.
Denser infill keeps a warm part from slowly collapsing under load.

materialHints.note: Carbon fiber does not rescue PLA: PLA-CF softens near 50 C.

changes.why: Thicker layers mean fewer layers. 0.24 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle matches Bambu's Draft preset.
Infill is hidden, so keep it at the stock 15 percent.
Grid is one of the fastest patterns and is the Bambu default.
Four top layers still close the surface at thicker layer heights, as in Bambu's Draft preset.
Prints sparse infill every second layer at double height, which saves time inside the part.
0.28 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle is Bambu's Extra Draft height. Layer lines show, and that is fine for a test fit.
Two walls are enough for a shape check.
Lightning infill only holds up the top surfaces and uses the least plastic. Use it for looks only, never for load.
Lightning at low density is enough to carry the top skin.
Only the steepest overhangs get support, as in Bambu's Extra Draft preset.

advice.text: A 0.6 mm nozzle at 0.30 mm layers moves much more plastic per pass. Bambu ships 0.30 mm Standard and Strength presets for it. Suggest it for large parts when one is available (hardened steel handles every material).
High flow filament and a high flow hotend raise the melt limit. Bambu PETG HF runs 21 mm3/s on a standard X1C hotend and 29 on the high flow one.
Split the job across idle printers with the same material before cutting quality.

strength.label: Strong

changes.why: Walls carry most of the load. Four walls held 33 kg in CNC Kitchen's hook test where two walls held 20 kg.
25 percent infill backs up the walls without much extra time. Bambu's Strength preset uses the same value.
Gyroid is about equally strong in every direction, so the part does not have a weak axis.
Thicker top skins spread point loads from screws and clips.
A thicker base stops the first layers from cracking under a bolt head.
Layers bond best near the upper end of the filament's range. PLA peaked at 230 C and PETG at 245 C in layer adhesion tests; hotter than that gets weaker again.
Keeps every layer between about 30 and 50 percent of the nozzle, the band where layers bond best; parts weaken once layers pass half the nozzle.
Six walls make most small parts nearly solid where it counts. This matches Bambu's Strength preset.
Wider inner walls bond better. Layer adhesion peaked near 150 percent of nozzle width, and the outside of the part looks the same.
Wider infill lines are stronger and print in fewer passes.
Past this point walls give more strength per gram than more infill.
A slower outer wall lays down a denser, more even skin. Bambu's Strength preset runs it at 60 mm/s.
An extra wall every other layer wedges the infill between walls for a stronger bond. Orca requires turning off ensure vertical shell thickness with it.
Required by alternate extra wall.

change.why: Less part cooling keeps each layer hot long enough to fuse with the next.

materialHints.note: PLA is stiff and strong but brittle and creeps under steady load or warmth. PETG is tougher. For heat or long term load, step up to ASA, PC or nylon composites.

advice.text: Lay the part so the load runs along the layers, never across them. Lying samples reached about 60 MPa in PLA while layer to layer bonds peaked at 40 MPa.
For brackets and hooks, print on the side so the bend is in the XY plane.

checks: In preview, confirm walls reach the requested count on thin features (Arachne may merge them).
Estimate time again. More walls and hotter temperatures can push the job past a deadline; see tradeoffs.

changes.why: Thin layers go where stair steps show on curves and shallow slopes; vertical walls stay thicker and faster.
Thinner layers make the steps on curves smaller. Bambu's High Quality presets start at 0.16 mm.
A slow outer wall shows fewer ripples and more even gloss. Bambu's High Quality presets use 60 mm/s.
Gentler acceleration on the visible wall cuts ringing near corners.
Matches Bambu's High Quality presets, which trade time for a calmer surface.
A slower top skin lies flatter.
A scarf seam ramps the start and end of each outer loop so the seam line nearly disappears and gets stronger.
Lines the seam up toward the back of the part where it is least visible.
Inner, outer, inner wall order needs at least three walls.
The outer wall prints undisturbed from an inner wall for the best finish. Overhangs get slightly worse, so skip this on parts with steep overhangs.
Monotonic lines all run the same way, so the top reflects light evenly.
Leaves more room for the top pattern on flat faces, so tops look like one continuous sheet.
0.08 mm layers make lines almost invisible, at a large time cost. Bambu's 0.08 mm High Quality preset.
Ironing runs the hot nozzle over the top surface a second time to smooth it. Works only on flat tops.
Orca's default 10 percent flow fills the tiny gaps without ridges.
Orca default spacing, well under the nozzle width.
Orca default. Slow passes iron best.

advice.text: Face the most visible side away from supports and keep it vertical or on top. Support contact always leaves marks.
For a glossy or textured bottom face, pick the plate for the look: smooth PEI for glossy, textured PEI for a grain.

changes.why: Thick walls keep water out of the infill and survive years of sun cycling.
A closed top skin stops rain from pooling inside the part.
Seals the base against standing water.
Prints the outer wall as one continuous spiral with no seam.
Vase mode prints a single wall.
There is no inside to fill.
The top stays open.
Vase mode cannot print supports.
A solid floor of three or more layers. Raise it for planters or anything holding water.
A wider single line (0.6 mm on a 0.4 mm nozzle) makes the wall stronger and watertight.
Smooths the XY moves too, so no seam shows even on sloped walls.

materialNotes.pla_silk: Silk PLA is the classic vase material. Keep its low max volumetric speed; the wall speed is capped by melt rate anyway.
materialNotes.petg: Good for planters and outdoor vases. Wide lines seal well.

constraints.text: One object per plate. Multiple objects print one at a time or not at all.
The model must be a solid. A model with its own inner wall prints both surfaces.
Layer time gets short near a narrow top. Keep minimum layer time on so the rim does not sag.

changes.why: Prusa recommends 3 to 4 walls for a watertight single wall, more for tricky shapes.
5 to 10 C above the preset fuses lines together with no pinholes. Stay inside the filament's range.
About 5 percent more plastic closes the tiny gaps between lines.
0.15 to 0.2 mm layers bond most reliably. Keep layers under about 60 percent of the nozzle width.
Prusa suggests 25 to 35 percent overlap between infill and walls if a part leaks.
Closes lids and tops fully.
The floor of a container takes the pressure; five solid layers seal it.
Adds solid infill under sloped walls so the shell never gets thin.
Scarf seams overlap the start and end of each loop, so the seam is not a weak line where water gets in.

materialHints.note: PETG bonds layers very well and is a common choice. ASA and ABS can also be sealed with an acetone vapor or wipe.

pairs.resolution: Keep the walls and the temperature from strength (they are cheap in time and carry the load). Take layer height and infill pattern from speed. Infill density goes to the strength floor, not the speed ceiling.
pairs.never: Never use lightning infill for a part that carries load.
pairs.tellUser: Kept four walls for strength and used thicker layers to save time.

pairs.resolution: Both can hold. Slow only the outer wall; inner walls and infill stay fast. Wall order inner, outer, inner still gives strong walls.
They pull opposite ways on walls and infill. Ask which matters more. A tough but bendy part usually means TPU 95A with three walls.
pairs.ask: Should it bend and spring back, or hold its shape under load?

pairs.resolution: Vase mode is one line thick. Refuse the combination unless the user accepts a fragile part; offer a wide line (1.5 times the nozzle) or normal mode with two walls and no top.
pairs.ask: Vase mode makes a single wall. Do you want the seamless look or a stronger part?

pairs.resolution: Keep walls, cut infill. Walls give the most strength per gram.
Slow only the outer wall and the top surface. Everything hidden runs at speed. Layer height is the real conflict: offer 0.16 mm as the middle ground.
Detail needs thin layers, which are slow. Keep 0.08 to 0.12 mm and save time by batching several models per plate instead.
pairs.tellUser: Fine layers take time. Printing several at once is the fastest way to more models.

pairs.resolution: Slow only the outer wall. Keep compensation settings; they cost nothing.
Keep walls, flow and temperature from watertight. Vase mode is both fast and seamless if the shape allows it.
Compatible. Use vase mode with a line width of at least 1.5 times the nozzle and five bottom layers.
Heat resistance picks the material first. If the loaded spool cannot meet the use temperature, stop and propose a material before changing settings.
Same as heat resistance: the material decides. ASA needs an enclosure; check the printer before planning.
Never drops the caveats. Food contact never unlocks materials outside its prefer list without an explicit user confirmation.

flow_ratio.why: Best block from the flow test.

input_shaping.why: Stay under the acceleration the shaper recommends, or ringing returns.

max_volumetric_speed.why: Measured limit minus 15 percent headroom so strength and quality hold.

pressure_advance.why: Use the calibrated value from the filament profile.
Best row or height from the test.

retraction.why: Shortest length that printed clean. Saved as the filament's retraction override.

temperature.why: Start the first layer at the same temperature unless the profile already runs it 5 to 10 C lower.

tolerance.why: Positive values open holes up by the measured error.
Corrects outside dimensions by the measured error.
